materials.title: Calling the skating centre
materials.text:
Woman: West Street Skating Centre. How can I help?
Tim: Hello. Do you have a class for beginners on Saturday?
Woman: Yes. It starts at ten and finishes at eleven.
Tim: I'm nine. Can I join?
Woman: Children from eight to twelve can join. Please come at 9:40 to get ready.
Tim: I don't have skates. Is that a problem?
Woman: No. You can borrow them here. Tell us your shoe size when you book.
Tim: What should I wear?
Woman: Long trousers and a top with long sleeves. We provide the safety equipment.
Tim: Can Dad watch?
Woman: Yes, from the seats upstairs. He cannot stand on the skating area during class.
Tim: How much is the lesson?
Woman: Seven pounds, including the borrowed skates.
Tim: Thank you. Dad will book my place.

questions.prompt: When does the class begin?
questions.explanation: Ten is class start. 9:40 is preparation arrival and eleven finish.

questions.prompt: Can nine-year-old Tim join?
questions.explanation: The class accepts ages8–12, including nine. Adults-only and twelve-only rules are false.

questions.prompt: What should Tim tell the centre when booking?
questions.explanation: Shoe size helps provide borrowed skates. Songs and birthdays are not requested.

questions.prompt: Where may Dad watch?
questions.explanation: The upstairs seats are allowed; the skating area is prohibited and a cupboard not offered.

questions.prompt: What does the seven-pound price include?
options: Only a new pair of skates to keep
questions.explanation: Borrowed skates are included with the lesson. No permanent purchase or lunch is included.

materials.title: A call to the repair shop
materials.text:
Man: Needle and Thread. Can I help?
Ella: Hello. Can you mend a zip on a school bag?
Man: Usually, yes. Bring the bag so we can look at it first.
Ella: Are you open after school today?
Man: We close at six. Tomorrow we close at four.
Ella: Can you finish it while I wait?
Man: I cannot promise before seeing it. If it is a small problem, it may be quick.
Ella: Where is your shop?
Man: Beside the bakery, opposite the post office.
Ella: Should I take everything out of the bag?
Man: Yes, please. Bring it empty, and put your name on a small note inside.
Ella: How will I know when it is ready?
Man: We can call a parent. Ask them which number we should use.
Ella: Thank you. I'll come with Mum before six.

questions.prompt: What does Ella want repaired?
options: A zip on a school bag
questions.explanation: She asks about the school-bag zip. The wheel and window are not her repair.

questions.prompt: When does the shop close today?
questions.explanation: Today closing is six; four applies tomorrow and noon is not given.

questions.prompt: Can the man promise to repair it immediately?
options: Yes, every repair takes one minute
Only if Ella leaves the bag full
No, he must see it first
questions.explanation: He explicitly cannot promise until seeing it. A universal one-minute repair and a full bag are not the conditions.

questions.prompt: Where is the shop?
questions.explanation: It is beside the bakery and opposite the post office. The other locations are not stated.

questions.prompt: How should Ella bring the bag?
options: Empty, with her name on a note
questions.explanation: The man asks for an empty bag and name note. Full books contradict the request; she will come with Mum.

materials.title: Badger’s very long title
materials.text:
In a town of talking animals, Badger wrote a play. He gave it a wonderful title: "The Amazing Adventure of the Brave Little Beetle Who Found a Silver Key beside the River."

Badger painted every word on a poster. By the time he reached the last line, the letters were tiny. He put the poster outside the hall and waited for visitors.

Mouse stopped to read it but had to move very close. Rabbit hurried past because she could not see what the poster was about. Badger felt disappointed. He had worked hard on every letter.

Owl asked what a passer-by needed to know first. Badger answered, "That there is a play, and when it starts."

They made a new poster. The large title was "The Silver Key". Under it, Badger wrote the day, time and place. His longer title stayed on the programme inside the hall.

That evening, Rabbit returned with two friends. She could read the new poster from across the path. Badger did not decide that long titles were always bad. He had learned that different places needed different amounts of information.

questions.prompt: What problem did the first poster have?
options: The letters became too small to read easily
It showed the wrong river on a map
It contained no words at all
questions.explanation: The long title forces tiny letters. The poster has many words, and no map is described.

questions.prompt: Why did Rabbit hurry past at first?
options: She had already watched the play twice
She could not quickly see what it was about
She was angry about a silver key
questions.explanation: She could not understand the poster from passing distance. Prior attendance and anger are not stated.

questions.prompt: What did Owl ask Badger to think about?
options: What passers-by needed to know first
How to make every letter smaller
How to hide the starting time
questions.explanation: Owl asks for essential initial information. Concealing time or shrinking letters would worsen the problem.

questions.prompt: Where did Badger keep the long title?
options: On the programme inside the hall
questions.explanation: The longer title remains on the programme. Street placement and a pocket are not given.

questions.prompt: What did Badger learn?
options: Information should fit the place and purpose
Every long title is always bad
Posters should never show a time
questions.explanation: He explicitly avoids a universal ban and learns about different information needs. The improved poster includes the time.

materials.title: The pot with the old marks
materials.text:
Mia borrowed a large plant pot from her aunt for a school display. The pot was clean, but there were old blue paint marks on one side. Mia thought they looked untidy.

She wanted to paint the whole pot white. Before opening the paint, she called her aunt to ask. Her aunt was glad she had checked. Mia's cousin had painted those blue marks when he was little, and the family wanted to keep them.

At first, Mia worried that the pot would spoil the display. Her teacher suggested turning the marked side towards the back, without changing the pot itself. They placed the school sign in front and added the plant.

The display looked good. At the end of the day, Mia returned the pot with all its marks still there. Her aunt showed her a photograph of her cousin holding a paintbrush beside it years earlier.

Mia understood why the marks mattered. They were not just dirt to remove. She was pleased that a simple phone call had protected something she had not known about. The next time she borrowed an object, she asked before making it look different.

questions.prompt: Why did Mia borrow the pot?
questions.explanation: The opening gives the school-display purpose. Sale and replacing a brush are not planned.

questions.prompt: Why did her aunt want to keep the blue marks?
options: They showed the price of the pot
They were needed for the plant to grow
They were a memory of Mia’s cousin painting as a child
questions.explanation: The childhood paintwork has family meaning. Price and growth are not reasons.

questions.prompt: What did the teacher suggest?
options: Break the pot into smaller pieces
Turn the marked side towards the back
questions.explanation: Turning preserves the pot while arranging the display. Repainting and breaking would change it against the owner’s wishes.

questions.prompt: What did Mia return?
options: The pot with its marks unchanged
questions.explanation: All marks remain. She neither paints white nor substitutes a photo.

questions.prompt: What did the phone call help Mia do?
options: Avoid changing something important to its owner
Discover that the pot was dirty
Find a cheaper plant to buy
questions.explanation: Asking protects a family memory. The pot was already clean and no plant price issue arises.

materials.title: Four holiday postcards
materials.text:
Four classmates send postcards during the same holiday week. Read what each person says. The weather describes that person's visit, not a rule about the place throughout the year.

Writer | Place | Weather during the visit | Main activity | Next plan
Amy | Lake Town | Sunny and warm | A boat trip with her parents | Visit the small history museum on Tuesday
Ben | Hill Village | Cool and cloudy | Walking on marked paths with his uncle | Try the indoor climbing wall on Wednesday
Chloe | Harbour City | Rainy | Drawing boats from a café window | Take a harbour tour if the weather improves
Daniel | Forest Camp | Dry in the day, cold at night | Nature activities with a school group | Return home on Friday morning

Amy says her boat left at ten and came back before lunch. Ben writes that the village shop closes early, so his uncle bought supplies in the morning. Chloe has not booked the harbour tour yet; she is waiting for the forecast. Daniel asks his family to keep his thick blanket ready at home because he wants a warm evening after the camp.

The classmates will share their photographs at school next week. Nobody has to print every picture: each person should choose three and be ready to explain one.

questions.prompt: Who is drawing boats from indoors?
questions.explanation: Chloe draws from a café window. Amy takes a boat trip and Daniel joins camp activities.

questions.prompt: Why has Chloe not booked the tour?
options: The tour is always free on Friday
She is waiting to see whether the weather improves
questions.explanation: She explicitly waits for a better forecast. Return and a Friday fee rule are not given.

questions.prompt: When does Daniel plan to return?
questions.explanation: His next plan is Friday morning. Tuesday/Wednesday belong to other classmates’ plans.

questions.prompt: What should each student choose for school?
options: Only a postcard with no explanation
questions.explanation: The final instruction is three photos and an explanation of one. Printing everything and no explanation contradict it.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported?
options: Forest Camp is always warm at night
The weather reports concern these visits
Harbour City is rainy every day of every year
questions.explanation: The opening limits the reports to the visit. Universal rain and permanent warm nights are unsupported; Daniel’s nights are cold.

materials.title: Four language-club projects
materials.text:
The language club is holding a project afternoon next Thursday. Students may visit two projects, choosing times that allow movement between rooms. Each presentation lasts twenty minutes, followed by ten minutes for questions. All rooms are on the ground floor.

Project | Start | Room | What visitors will see
Words on Wheels | 13:00 | Room A | A poster about useful language on buses and trains
Stories in Two Voices | 13:30 | Room B | A short story read by two speakers with different parts
Food Words at Home | 14:00 | Room C | A display of family food words, with permission from contributors
Signs around Us | 14:30 | Room A | Photographs of public signs and explanations of their purposes

Visitors should arrive before a presentation begins and stay until its question time ends. Move quietly between rooms. No booking is needed, but a room may close its door when all seats are taken.

Food Words at Home is a language display, not a tasting session. Please do not bring food to share unless a teacher has arranged it separately. Students appearing in any photograph have already agreed to its use. Visitors should ask before taking close-up pictures of another student's work.

After visiting, write one question or idea on the feedback board in the hall. It should refer to a project, not judge a classmate's personal appearance. The club wants comments that help the next group improve its explanation.

questions.prompt: Where is Stories in Two Voices?
questions.explanation: The table assigns it Room B. Room A hosts two other projects and Room C the food-language display.

questions.prompt: When does Food Words at Home begin?
questions.explanation: Its start is14:00. The other times belong to Stories and Signs.

questions.prompt: What will happen at Food Words at Home?
options: A language display without an arranged tasting
questions.explanation: The notice explicitly distinguishes the language display from tasting. No universal meal or competition is offered.

questions.prompt: What should visitors do before photographing another student’s work closely?
options: Assume all work can be photographed without permission
questions.explanation: Visitors must ask. The existing permission for appearing in a photo does not grant unlimited new close-ups of work.

questions.prompt: What kind of feedback does the club want?
options: A judgment about a classmate’s appearance
Only a list of room colours
questions.explanation: The board seeks comments improving explanations. Personal appearance judgments are excluded and room colours alone do not address projects.
